source.title: Assessment of Skeletal Muscle Contractile Properties by Radial Displacement: The Case for Tensiomyography

paper.citation: Macgregor, L. J., Hunter, A. M., Orizio, C., Fairweather, M. M., & Ditroilo, M. (2018). Assessment of skeletal muscle contractile properties by radial displacement: The case for tensiomyography. Sports Medicine, 48(7), 1607–1620. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-018-0912-6
paper.abstract: What physiological construct, validity, reliability, and applied evidence support tensiomyography? Narrative measurement review spanning healthy adults, cadaver-matched samples, athletes, and exercise studies. No pooled population or quantitative synthesis. Athlete-monitoring transfer depends on muscle, protocol, state, operator, and outcome. Narrative review of TMG mechanisms, parameters, validity, reliability, exercise responses, and applications. Does not report a systematic search or formal risk-of-bias assessment. TMG electrically stimulates muscle and records radial displacement with a digital sensor.
paper.tldr: This review provides a measurement-focused basis for interpreting TMG parameters and their limits in athlete monitoring. Contraction time correlated with type-I fiber proportion in several small studies, including r = 0.88 in a same-participant biopsy study of 27 people. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Narrative review of TMG mechanisms, parameters, validity, reliability, exercise responses, and applications. Does not report a systematic search or formal risk-of-bias assessment. TMG electrically stimulates muscle and records radial displacement with a digital sensor.
paper.findings: Contraction time correlated with type-I fiber proportion in several small studies, including r = 0.88 in a same-participant biopsy study of 27 people. Short-term/inter-rater studies often reported ICCs above 0.86, but electrode distance and sensor placement altered measurements. Longer-term reliability was weaker and state dependent: Dm CV 8.0–14.8% and Tc CV 3.8–9.4%, while half-relaxation time CV reached 27.8–32.7%. The authors identified Dm and Tc as the most reliable commonly used parameters but noted unresolved external validity in elite and clinical populations.
paper.limitations: Criterion validity is difficult, and no study had directly compared Dm with in-vivo muscle stiffness at the time of review. Parameter definitions, including contraction velocity, were not standardized. Reliability and validity in specialist athlete and patient populations were not established. Narrative synthesis and small construct-validation samples limit certainty.
paper.practicalImplications: TMG can describe standardized evoked radial-displacement responses, but labels such as stiffness, fatigue, or fiber type should remain qualified. Use muscle- and protocol-specific reliability, lock sensor/electrode placement, and avoid turning TMG changes into readiness or injury claims without external validation.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. TMG can describe standardized evoked radial-displacement responses, but labels such as stiffness, fatigue, or fiber type should remain qualified. Use muscle- and protocol-specific reliability, lock sensor/electrode placement, and avoid turning TMG changes into readiness or injury claims without external validation. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, tMG can describe standardized evoked radial-displacement responses, but labels such as stiffness, fatigue, or fiber type should remain qualified. Use muscle- and protocol-specific reliability, lock sensor/electrode placement, and avoid turning TMG changes into readiness or injury claims without external validation. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
